messages.subject: Correlation
messages.body_plain:
I asked a question regarding the meaning of the Correlation statement
that follows Fixed effects in the lme output.  I thank Drs. Jones,
Dubin, and Pinheiro for their help.  They provided the following
information:

------------------------------------------------------------------------
----------
No, this just lists the estimated correlations between fixed effects
estimates; (Intr) is an abbreviation for (Intercept), which must be a
fixed effect included in your model.

Hope this helps,
--José

José Pinheiro
Biostatistics, Novartis Pharmaceuticals
One Health Plaza, Room 419/2115             office: (973) 781-8879
East Hanover, NJ 07936                      fax:    (973) 781-6498
------------------------------------------------------------------------
------------
 Hello,

    That refers to the correlation between the fixed effects (population
average) intercept estimate [Intr] and the other fixed effects parameter
estimates from the lme fit.  All such unique pairwise correlations
between the fixed effects parameter estimates are presented.  To get the
intraclass correlation estimate for a random intercept model, you will
need to use the standard deviation estimates of the random intercept and
within-subject error that are output from the lme fit.

    Sincerely, Joel.

Joel Dubin
Assistant Professor
Division of Biostatistics
Department of Epidemiology and Public Health
Yale University
joel.dubin at yale.edu
------------------------------------------------------------------------
--------------
Yes,
If you can get hold of Pinheiro & Bates (2000) "Mixed Effects Models in
S and S-Plus" they explain lme in detail.

messages.subject: Summary: NAs in eigen
messages.body_plain:
Dear Splus-users,

Great thanks to Prof Ripley for the helpful
reply which is attached below.

Best,
Chunlei Ke

===
> From: Prof Brian D Ripley <ripley at stats.ox.ac.uk>
> To: Chunlei KE <ke97 at hotmail.com>
> CC: s-news at lists.biostat.wustl.edu
> Subject: Re: [S] NAs in eigen
> Date: Thu, 28 Feb 2002 08:47:19 +0000 (GMT)
>
> On Wed, 27 Feb 2002, Chunlei KE wrote:
>
>
>
> > Dear Splus-users,
> >
> > I tried to use eigen() to calculate eigen values for a symetric matrix,
> > and came across the following:
> >
> > >is.matrix(mat)
> > [1] T
> > >dim(mat)
> > [1] 252 252
> > >summary(mat)
> >   Min. 1st Qu. Median    Mean 3rd Qu. Max.
> > -0.25   -0.25  -0.25 0.00154    0.75 0.75
> >
> > >eigen(mat)$value
> >   [1]          NA          NA          NA          NA  6.795e+001
> > 1.612e-014  2.572e-016 ... ...
> >
> > These NA's are wrong. But eigen.Matrix gives the
> > correct answer:
> >
> > >Re(eigen.Matrix(mat)$value) # imaginary part is very small
> >   [1]  6.300e+001  6.795e+001  5.805e+001  2.654e-016  2.654e-016
> > 1.900e-015 ...
>
> Is this then a non-symmetric matrix with 3 non-zero real eigenvalues?
> It really is asking rather a lot of an eigenvalue routine to cope with a
> 252-dimensional matrix with that degree of numerical singularity,
> and unusual to have some much structure and not exploit it.
>
> > I am using Splus 2000 on NT. I tried on unix (Splus 3.4) and it has no
> > problem, either.
>
> `unix' isn't very precise: this sort of thing depends on the compiler
> and the run-time libraries. Different Unices often give different answers.
>
> > Can someone please tell me what happened to these NAs? Is there any
> > way to go around(in this example, those NAs are 0's indeed)?
>
> I think you have already used it: eigen.Matrix is based on LAPACK and is a
> better algorithm than that underlying eigen.  Unfortunately the current
> version of S-PLUS for Windows does not have library(Matrix). Often an even
> better alternative is to use the SVD and not the eigendecomposition: but
> that depends on the problem.
>
> --
> Brian D. Ripley,                  ripley at stats.ox.ac.uk
> Professor of Applied Statistics,  http://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~ripley/

messages.subject: Re: comparing longitudinal data
messages.body_plain:
Hello all-

I am trying to plot the a continuous variable with respect to time.  I have
three arms that I wish to compare, whereby each arm has approximately 150
subjects, each having from 1-n different observations of the continuous
variable (x). Observations were not collected at the same time points for
each subject.  Essentially this a repeated measures at irregular time
points question.

My first crack at attempting to plot the time vs. the variable x was to
break the data apart by using the tapply function breaking the data apart
by arbitrary time intervals and computing the mean value for each arm at
these time intervals.  Next I used the plot function and the lines function
to plot all three arms showing the change in the measured parameter as a
function of time.  This is a very crude approach, which results in a loss
of data and does not account for the decreased number of subjects over
time, i.e. all 450 have at least 1 observation of x, but less have 10
observations, etc.

Does anyone have any other methods that help to analyze these type of
irregular continuous data?

Many thanks in advance

LaRee

messages.subject: Avoiding for() loops
messages.body_plain:
The following function takes n = how.many *randomly-sized* random samples
from p, in which the probability of selection for p[i] depends on the value
of k[i] relative to max(k) -- thus, if max(k) = k[m], p[m] is selected for
every sample.

CJ.sample <- function(p, k, how.many){

        how.big <- length(p)
        
        coins <- k/max(k)
        index <- matrix(nrow=how.big, ncol=how.many)
        samples <- matrix(nrow=how.big, ncol=how.many)

        for (i in 1:how.big)
                for (j in 1:how.many)
                        index[i,j] <- ifelse(runif(1,0,1)<=coins[i], TRUE,
FALSE)

# tosses "coins" to determine membership of "samples"

        for (i in 1:how.big)
                for (j in 1:how.many)
                        samples[i,j] <- ifelse(index[i,j]==T,
test.frame$p[i], NA)

# creates samples

        samples
}

I realise that for() loops should be avoided wherever possible and the
apply() group of functions used instead, but after a lot of thought I'm
still at a loss as to how to do so in this case; perhaps I have been staring
at it too long (or I've too little experience of S-Plus).

Since length(p) will typically be of the order of 5*10^4, and it has been
suggested that a suitable number of samples might be 100, a more efficient
method is rather urgent.

All suggestions -- including (specific) ones for further study -- gratefully
received.

messages.subject: Summary (2): Specifying a primary split on a regression tree
messages.subject_clean: Summary (2): Specifying a primary split on a regression tree
messages.body_plain:
This is an addendum to a summary that I posted last week.  After I reported in my original summary that I was still seeking a solution, several of you jumped right in and tried to help me.  I'm thankful for your efforts.

Particular thanks to Greg Snow, Marc Feldesman, Don McKenzie, and Terry Therneau for providing assistance with my tree issue.  Dr. Snow wrote and shared a script with me that did exactly what I was interested in.  One of the challenges I faced was having both numeric and factor variables as potential splits and this was also accommodated in Dr. Snow's script.  Terry Therneau suggested that I could also use the latest version of rpart to address my issue.  I include the original question and the two solutions below (I did not test Terry Therneau's approach).

Michael Wing

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>

My original post:

> I'm using S-Plus 2000 (Release 3) to create regression trees and am

> interested in investigating surrogate splits.  I would like to explicitly

> specify a primary split from my candidate variables and allow the software

> to create trees based on this primary split.  Any suggestions would be

> welcome.

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>

The solution as provided by Dr. Snow:

fit.fuel <- tree(Mileage ~ Weight+Disp.+Type, fuel.frame)# creates the tree

burl1 <- burl.tree(fit.fuel, 1, plot=F) #establishes burl plot for examining other splits

tempnames <- c("Weight","Disp.","Type")# list of variables to examine as primary splits

fuel.fits <- list()#create an empty list to store other fits

#loop to create tree objects for each primary split

for (i in tempnames){

        cat( "woring on ",i,"\n")

        tempmat <- burl1[[i]]

        dev.max <- max(tempmat[,2])

        if( is.factor(fuel.frame[[i]]) ){

                 var.val <- tempmat[ tempmat[,2] == dev.max, 4:5]

                 fuel.fits[[i]] <- edit.tree(fit.fuel, 1, i, var.val[[1]],

                                             var.val[[2]])

        } else {

        var.val <- tempmat[ tempmat[,2] == dev.max, 1 ]

        fuel.fits[[i]] <- edit.tree(fit.fuel, 1, i, var.val)

        }

}

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>

An alternate solution as provided by Terry Therneau:

 What you need is the just-done release of rpart, which has two new parameters.

        1. Variable costs.  The best split is chosen as the one with minimal

                cost*impurity

        2. Max depth for a tree.

        

If your variables are binary, then setting the cost for the chosen one to

.001 and the others to 1 would do it.  If they are continuous, the

strategy would be to first fit a tree with maxdepth=1 (one split), and

the cost for the chosen variable set to .0001 or similar, with cost 1 for the

others.  Then predict(fit) will create for you a new yes/no variable that

encodes this best split.  Then rerun with that new binary variable as the

low cost one.

messages.subject_clean: Survival Curves for covariate measurement error
messages.body_plain:
I am currently analyzing some complicated 
data.  There are four groups of rabbits,

a control group and three treatment dose 
groups.  The treatment consists of an

antibacterial agent.  Every group of 
rabbits has been exposed to the same 
infectious 

agent.  (So far, so good.)  
However, there are some substantial dosing 
errors for the 

infectious agent - if an "average" dose 
consists of 3.0 x 10^6 bacteria per liter 
of air, 

then the doses can vary anwhere from 5.0 x 
10^5 to 8.0 x 10^6 bacteria per liter.

(The median lethal dose for this particular 
infectious agent is rather high, and the 

estimated logit lethality model for the 
agent has a very flat slope - consequently, using large

doses is a reasonable thing to do.)  Three of the rabbits are censored, as they survived 

beyond the two week observation period.

 

My knowledge of survival analysis is mostly 
parametric (J.F. Lawless, for example)

but I am familiar with standard 
nonparametric techniques as well.  I am unaware of

"standard" techniques for analyzing survival 
data in which the most important covariate

is subject to substantial errors, and any 
recommendations for a reasonable 
approach

would be greatly appreciated.

Regards, 

David Alan Paul, Ph.D.

messages.subject: Re: GAM - negative binomial
messages.body_plain:
Dear Nestor,

 

Some years ago Ari Verbyla and I looked at fitting 
gam's with negative binomial errors and we did make some progress.  I never 
followed it through, though, because of a couple of tricky issues that 
I did never satisfactorily resolve.  GAM estimation is, of course, not 
maximum likelihood.  The likelihood is penalized, essentially to ensure 
that the smooth terms do not consume too many degrees of freedom, and hence that 
they do remain "smooth".  This itself makes inference on GAM models at 
least non-standard; you can't just assume that normal likelihood ratio theory 
will go through smoothly.  Secondly the penalty term makes the likelihood 
very similar (in some cases mathematically identical) to a random effects 
model.  The negative binomial can already be viewed as a Poisson model with 
a simple random effect attacted to each term.  This mixing of random 
effects and penalty terms seems to make things a bit slippery.  My view is 
that if you really want to go this way it would be better to formulate a full 
Poisson GLMM and be done with it.  Just my view.

 

The 
other point I would make is that I have found in practice that the full 
apparatus of GAM's is not all that necessary.  I have had pretty good 
success just fitting splines with a fixed number of degrees of freedom in an 
ordinary GLM, thus avoiding the penalty apparatus.  I'm not saying that 
this will always work, but you might find it useful to give it a try.  It 
makes life much easier if it comes off.

 

Bill Venables.

Just solve the Yule-Walker equations for gamma (the autocorrelations):
See Brockwell & Davis (1991), around eqn (3.3.8).

The next version of R (available as R-devel now) will have a function
ARMAacf to do this for a general ARMA process, and the code will
(almost) run in S-PLUS.  There is also function armacorr in timeslab
(in the S section on statlib).

messages.subject: SUMMARY: Avoiding for() loops
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Bill Dunlap, Nick Ellis, Steve McKinney, Brian Ripley, Dimitris
Rizopoulos and Greg Warnes for their replies.

I've learnt a lot from their various approaches (reproduced below); the
essential lesson in this case seems to be that appropriate indexing works
wonders -- see Bill's solution especially. This takes slightly less than six
seconds on a Pentium III for a dataset of 5*10^5 and 100 samples. A similar
use of indexing, but which involves looping over the 100 samples, still only
takes around 16 seconds.

Julian Wells

++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++

Bill Dunlap
=======

The goal is not to avoid for loops in favor of calls to lapply or apply;
it is to minimize the number of function calls.  A simple transformation is
the change the loop
                for (j in 1:how.many)
                        index[i,j] <- ifelse(runif(1,0,1)<=coins[i], TRUE,
FALSE)
to the single call to runif()
                index[i,] <- runif(how.many, 0, 1) <= coins[i]
(The ifelse was not ever needed.)

I think the following does about what your code does.  (I guessed at
some reasonable types for the arguments.)

CJ.sample1
function(p = letters[1:4], k = 1:4, how.many = 10)
{
        how.big <- length(p)
        coins <- k/max(k)
        samples <- matrix(p, nrow = how.big, ncol = how.many)
        samples[runif(how.many * how.big) > coins] <- NA
        samples
}

Nick Ellis:
=======

Try

index <-
sweep(matrix(runif(how.big*how.many),how.big,how.many),1,coins,"<=")

> # tosses "coins" to determine membership of "samples"
> 
>       for (i in 1:how.big)
>               for (j in 1:how.many)
>                       samples[i,j] <- ifelse(index[i,j]==T,
> test.frame$p[i], NA)
> 

Try

samples[index] <- p[row(index)[index]]

Steve McKinney
===========

### Here's one way to approach the problem.
### I modified your function as I presumed
### you meant p[i] where you had test.frame$p[i]

### So here's your function,

CJ.sample <-
  function(p, k, how.many, seed = .Random.seed)
{

  set.seed(seed)
  
  how.big <- length(p)
        
  coins <- k/max(k)
  index <- matrix(nrow=how.big, ncol=how.many)
  samples <- matrix(nrow=how.big, ncol=how.many)

  

  for (i in 1:how.big)
    for (j in 1:how.many)
      index[i,j] <- ifelse(runif(1,0,1)<=coins[i], TRUE,
                           FALSE)

  ## tosses "coins" to determine membership of "samples"

  for (i in 1:how.big)
    for (j in 1:how.many)
      samples[i,j] <- ifelse(index[i,j]==T,
                             p[i], NA)

  ## creates samples

  samples
}

### and here is a modified version

CJ.sample.2 <-
  function(p, k, how.many, seed = .Random.seed)
{

  if(length(p) != length(k)){
    stop("lengths of p and k must be the same")}
  
  how.big <- length(p)
  coins <- k/max(k)
  
  set.seed(seed)
  index <- matrix(runif(how.big*how.many, 0, 1),
                  nrow = how.big, byrow = T) > coins
  
  ## tosses "coins" to determine membership of "samples"

  samples <- matrix(p, nrow = how.big, ncol = how.many, byrow = F)
  samples[index] <- NA

  ## creates samples

  samples
}

### The tricks are
### 1) avoid for loops in random number generation -
###    generate all the numbers at once and save them in a
###    vector or matrix, or just use them right away as above.
### 2) Take advantage of the fact that you can fill matrices
###    with vectors, in row or column order.  The trick here is
###    setting up the index matrix properly with byrow = T,
###    but there are other ways of doing this such as with
###    transposing matrices with the t() function.
### 3) Use the subscripting power of S-PLUS to index an entire
###    matrix with another matrix of the same size, as in the
###    samples[index] <- NA command.

> set.seed(145)
> p <- 1:20
> k <- runif(length(p))
> n.samp <- 11
> 
> myseed <- 1055
> dos.time(foo <- CJ.sample(p, k, how.many = n.samp, seed = myseed))
[1] 2.9440000000004147
> dos.time(bar <- CJ.sample.2(p, k, how.many = n.samp, seed = myseed))
[1] 0.010000000000218279
> 
> all.equal(foo, bar)
[1] T
> 
> 
> set.seed(15)
> p <- 1:25
> k <- runif(length(p))
> n.samp <- 19
> 
> myseed <- 625
> dos.time(foo <- CJ.sample(p, k, how.many = n.samp, seed = myseed))
[1] 6.3190000000004147
> dos.time(bar <- CJ.sample.2(p, k, how.many = n.samp, seed = myseed))
[1] 0.020000000000436557
> 
> all.equal(foo, bar)
[1] T
> 
> ### Now try a big example, using the new function only.
> 
> set.seed(145)
> p <- 1:50000
> k <- runif(length(p))
> n.samp <- 100
> 
> myseed <- 1055
> 
> dos.time(bar <- CJ.sample.2(p, k, how.many = n.samp, seed = myseed))
[1] 12.347999999999956

### So you should be able to run your examples in a reasonable
### amount of time. 

Brian Ripley
========

runif(how.big) < k/max(k)

will select a sample with item i being selected with probability
proportional to k.  So I think for one sample you want

p[runif(how.big) < k/max(k)]

and a loop over 100 times would be fine.  It could be vectorized, but
you'll get some large objects doing so.

Dimitris Rizopoulos
=============

Hi,

You could use something like this:

k <- 1:10
coins <- k/max(k)
index <- matrix(coins,nrow=10, ncol=20)
out <- apply(index,2, function(x){
apply(as.matrix(x),1,function(y)
ifelse(runif(1,0,1)<=y, TRUE,FALSE))})

Greg Warnes
=========

First, it looks like you can combine the two for loops into a single loop
which should cut the time required to run the function by at least half:

CJ.sample.fix1 <- function(p, k, how.many){

        how.big <- length(p)
        
        coins <- k/max(k)
        index <- matrix(nrow=how.big, ncol=how.many)
        samples <- matrix(nrow=how.big, ncol=how.many)
 
        for (i in 1:how.big)
                for (j in 1:how.many)
               {
                        index[i,j] <- ifelse(runif(1,0,1)<=coins[i], TRUE,
FALSE)
                        samples[i,j] <- ifelse(index[i,j]==T, p[i], NA)
               }

      sample
 }

Second, note that ifelse, runinf and assignment are vectorized. This allows
the outermost loop to be done way with:

CJ.sample.fix2 <- function(p, k, how.many){

 how.big <- length(p)
 
  coins <- k/max(k)
  index <- matrix(nrow=how.big, ncol=how.many)
  samples <- matrix(nrow=how.big, ncol=how.many)
 
  for (j in 1:how.many)
      samples[,j] <- ifelse(runif(length(p),0,1) <= coins, p, NA )
           
  samples
 }

Finally, you should be able to see that this can be accomplished by using
sapply:

CJ.sample.fix3 <- function(p, k, how.many)
{
  
  how.big <- length(p)
  
  coins <- k/max(k)
  index <- matrix(nrow=how.big, ncol=how.many)
  samples <- matrix(nrow=how.big, ncol=how.many)

  sapply( 1:how.many, function(x) ifelse(runif(length(p),0,1) <= coins, p,
NA ) )
}

Here are the timings for a some small sized problems:

# Original Function
> unix.time( CJ.sample( 1:100, seq(0,100,length=100), 12) )
[1] 10.22  0.00 10.30  0.00  0.00
> unix.time( CJ.sample( 1:1000, seq(0,1000,length=100), 12) )
[1] 105.59   0.03 105.74   0.00   0.00

# Removing extra loop
> unix.time( CJ.sample.fix1( 1:100, seq(0,100,length=100), 12) )
[1] 10.21  0.00 10.21  0.00  0.00
> unix.time( CJ.sample.fix1( 1:1000, seq(0,1000,length=100), 12) )
[1] 105.76   0.00 105.92   0.00   0.00

# Replacing outer for with vectorized operations
> unix.time( CJ.sample.fix2( 1:100, seq(0,100,length=100), 12) )
[1] 0.06 0.00 0.06 0.00 0.00
> unix.time( CJ.sample.fix2( 1:1000, seq(0,1000,length=100), 12) )
[1] 0.1 0.0 0.1 0.0 0.0

# Replacing for with sapply
> unix.time( CJ.sample.fix3( 1:100, seq(0,100,length=100), 12) )
[1] 0.08 0.00 0.08 0.00 0.00
> unix.time( CJ.sample.fix3( 1:1000, seq(0,100,length=100), 12) )
[1] 0.1 0.0 0.1 0.0 0.0

I'm surprised to see that removing the extra set of loops had a trivial
effect.  But, as you can see, the best times are for .fix2 and .fix3 when
vectorize the outer loop.  This results in a speed gain of a couple orders
of magnitude, on these small problems, and will probably be even more on
your much larget problem.

messages.subject: SUMMARY: multiple processes/users
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks to Chuck Taylor, Vadim Kutsyy, Tony Plate, and James Holtman
for their helpful replies.   The consensus is to definitely not have
multiple
S-Plus processes concurrently writing to the same .Data directory.  One 
alternative is to have the processes write to different .Data directories, 
with a "combining" job at the end.

-Brad Mann  

----------------

Chuck Taylor 

It is very risky to have two S-PLUS processes concurrently working
in the same .Data directory.  We do not recommend it at all.  Each
process should have its own .Data directory. 

-------------------

Vadim Kutsyy

Attach this .Data so it will not be in the first place in search().  Then
you can save results to that .data using assign().  You don't want to run
multiple S processes from the same .Data.

---------------------

Tony Plate

You can do this, but as you say, you will get mixed results.  There are two 
reasons I know of: (1) S-plus caches objects, so an update to an object in 
one S-Plus process will be missed by the other S-Plus process, and (2) 
there are various "summary" objects in the database which an S-plus object 
needs a lock on to write.  If it can't get the lock, the necessary summary 
data (e.g., names of objects) may not be written.

Problem 1 can be often be circumvented by judicious use of 
synchronize(1).   However, in general, I would definitely avoid trying to 
run more than one S-plus process with the same active database (i.e., the 
same database in the first position of the search() list).

(It does work fine if the active database in one S-plus process is also 
being used in another S-plus process, but is further down the search list 
in that second S-plus process, so that the second S-plus process is never 
writing that database.  In that case, you just need to do synchronize(k) in 
the second S-plus process (where k is the index of the database in 
question) whenever the database is updated in the first S-plus process.)

------------------------

James Holtman

This is probably not a good idea.  All your objects are stored in the .Data
directory and if multiple processes are using the same objects, you will
probably get corrupted data in them.  I would suggest that if you are going
to have multiple sessions, then the .Data (first in the search path) should
be different for each session.  They can share common functions if these
are stored on the second (on down) entries of the search path.

If you are trying to "combine" the information, then have a separate
process that runs at the conclusion of the multiple processes that
'attaches' the other .Data directories and then does what ever combining
you want.  Since it is a single process, data won't get corrupted.

....

What you should do is to have each unique process that is started to have
its own unique instance of .Data in the first search position.  This is
where data is written to by default.  You can read data from any location
on the search path, so if you want to share data as read-only across the
processes, have it in any position but the first.  Reading should be OK
from any of the search positions.

You can even have all the processes have read-only access to the .Data
directories of the other processes, but you will still have some "race
conditions" if you are trying to read the objects since you might be
reading while the other process is writing.  I would avoid having to setup
a sitution where these processes are trying to share objects.

return (x)

messages.subject: Summary: saving multiple page graphs
messages.body_plain:
Greetings, All:

 

Earlier today I reported difficulty in saving and using all
the pages in a milti-page graph to make a Powerpoint file using S-Plus 2000
Pro.  It appears to be every bit as problematic as I found it to be.

 

Sundar Dorai-Raj suggested - 

 

Have you tried export.graph?
The problem though is it exports graphs as you create them. Therefore if you
have one graphsheet with 15 pages it will export the only the current graph.

 

Example.

 

export.graph(FileName="plots/export.wmf",Name="GSD2",ExportType="WMF")

 

or in a loop

 

for(1 in 1:15) {

  file.name <- paste("plots/export",i,".wmf",sep="")

  export.graph(FileName=file.name,Name="GSD2",ExportType="WMF")

}

 

The latter example results
in 15 images in the plot directory. However the graphsheet "GSD2" will
only contain the final plot. To avoid this you can create your plots on
separate graphsheets.

 

Sundar

 

 

The most useful solution came from Professor Bill Meeker,
and it works great BUT you have to have S-Plus 6 (which I have, although I use
S-Plus 2000 for other reasons).  Bill said to save the multipage graph in
2000, and then open it in 6.  Invoke the Powerpoint wizard and Bob’s
your uncle.

 

It worked great.

 

Thanks, Sundar and Bill!

 

 

Charles Annis, P.E.

www.StatisticalEngineering.com

561-352-9699

responses of each variable in a multivariate glm or gam - many thanks to
Tony Plate.

jane elith

>
>If I understand you correctly, the answer to your question is easy.  In a 
>GAM, the effect of each variable is independent of the values of other 
>variables; that's what makes it an additive model.  So plots for a GAM that 
>show the responses for each variable can be prepared independently for each 
>variable, and the total response of the GAM to an input vector is just the 
>sum of the responses to each variable.  E.g., when working out the data for 
>the plot of the response to the first variable, the values of the other 
>variables do not matter.
>
>

messages.body_plain:
On Tue, 12 Mar 2002, [iso-8859-1] Mäkinen Jussi wrote:

> Thx in advance, I guess that this question should put to a Windows group but
> I hope that You don't mind and somebody would have an answer and maybe
> solutions.
> 
> Is there any way to make a shortcut (Windows) to execute a splus script
> (open the program and execute a certain script)? What are the proper options
> if this is possible? Anything else that should be considered?
> 
> I would like to make the shortcut which would ease my colleques to benefit
> my scripts as well without a knowledge of S-plus itself. That's a question
> that would lie better to a windows group but 

The gory details are available in the programmers guide (ch. 18 S-PLUS 6,
ch. 19 S-PLUS 2000).

The short version is to use something like windows explorer and navigate
to the cmd directory of the S-PLUS instalation 
(c:\program files\sp2000\cmd or c:\program files\insightful\splus6\cmd)
find splus.exe and using the right mouse button drag it onto the desktop,
when you release the right button a small menu should pop-up, choose
"create shortcut here".  Now right click on the new icon and choose
properties.  Select tho shortcut tab.  In the target box it should have
the path to splus.exe, add the switch /BATCH to the end of it along with
the name of the file containing your script and optionally the name of the
file that you want the output to go to.  The box should end up looking
something like:

"c:\program files\insightful\splus6\cmd\splus.exe" /BATCH in.txt out.txt

you may want to also set some of the variables like S_PROJ.

Now if you double click on the icon it will start S-PLUS (but it will only
bring up a progress window, not the GUI) run the script and then exit.  If
you want it to bring up the GUI and run the script, but then continue
running so that you can do other things, leave out /BATCH and only include
the script file (no output file).

hope this helps,

--

messages.subject: Re: Stepwise regression
messages.body_plain:
All possible subsets regression in no way fixes these severe problems.
Things can even get worse - see

@ARTICLE{roe91pre,
  author = {Roecker, Ellen B.},
  year = 1991,
  title = {Prediction error and its estimation for subset-selected models},
  journal = {Technometrics},
  volume = 33,
  pages = {459-468}
}

To see the problems caused by all such approaches, randomly disassociate the Y 
vector from the X vectors - you'll get some "publishable" models.  Or use the 
bootstrap to show that the variables selected are almost completely random.

Frank Harrell

I am trying to understand the cause for warning messages generated
by discrim() but not with lda() [S+2000, Win2000]. For example, the 
following code with a random dataset:

p<-12 # number of variables
g<-3  # number of groups
n<-10 # number of observations/group
group<-sample(1:g,g*n,replace=T)
x<-matrix(runif(g*p*n),g*n,p)
fit<-discrim(factor(group)~.,data.frame(group,x),family=Classical("homo"))

yields the following warning messages:

Warning messages:
  Warning in discrim(factor(group) ~ ., data.frame(group, x), family: only
the first of 3 elements used for string value
Warning messages:
  Warning in discrim(factor(group) ~ ., data.frame(group, x), family:
Group(s) 1 have counts less than the number of variables= 12
Warning messages:
  Warning in discrim(factor(group) ~ ., data.frame(group, x), family: Rank
deficiency in group 1
Warning messages:
  Warning in discrim(factor(group) ~ ., data.frame(group, x), family: Rank
deficiency in group 2
Warning messages:
  Warning in discrim(factor(group) ~ ., data.frame(group, x), family: Rank
deficiency in group 3

the classification:

table(group,crossvalidate(fit)$groups)

is the same as the one obtained with lda() which does not generate any
message:

library("mass",first=T)
fit<-lda(x,factor(group),CV=T)
table(group,fit$class)

Some messages seems to be related to the fact that the number of 
parameters estimated in the covariance matrix (12*13/2=78) is larger than
the number of data (I don't undestand well the two first messagtes). As a 
matter of fact, when p=7, the number of parameters is 28 and there
is no warning message. However, when p=8 and the number of parameters
is 36, the apparition of the messages seems to depend on the dataset.

I have two questions:

1) what is prompting each one of the warning messages?

2) can I ignore them if I use cross-validation for the table?

Thank you for your help. 

Gabriel Baud-Bovy

messages.subject: Re: loess
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Don McKenzie and Bert Gunter.  Their responses are posted
below:

Check out some of the literature on the loess algorithm (you can start

with the Splus manuals or the chapter in Chambers & Hastie on local

regression models). There are no "regression coefficients" per
se, because 

loess() creates a number of local regression models on overlapping moving

windows of the data.

Chambers, J.M., and Hastie, T.J. (1991). Statistical Models in S,
309-376.

Cleveland, W.S., and Devlin, S.J., (1988) Locally-weighted Regression: An

Approach to Regression Analysis by Local Fitting. J. Am. Statist. Assoc.,

Vol. 83, pp 596-610.

_______________________________________________________________________

Don McKenzie, Quantitative Fire Ecologist 

Fire and Environmental Research Applications Team 

Seattle Forestry Sciences Lab, USDA Forest Service 

4043 Roosevelt Way NE 

Seattle, WA 98105-6497, USA

donaldmckenzie at fs.fed.us 

(206)732-7810; fax (541)732-7801

loess is a local fitting procedure that produces regression coefficients
for 

each local fit -- potentially hundreds of them for the many local fits
that 

are done. So there is little use or sense to providing the coefficients
-- 

and they aren't.

messages.body_plain:
Look at axis() in the help files. Below is an example:

# plot data but suppress default axes
plot(x=x,y=y,axes=F)
# add x-axis, round values to 1 decimal place
axis(side=1,at=pretty(x),labels=round(pretty(x),1))
# add default y-axis
axis(side=2)
# add surrounding box
box()

There may be other slicker solutions but this one works fine.

Sundar

categorical random (frailty) variable (V3).  V1 has three levels (Cazorla,
Magina and Caurel).  V5 has two (98 and 99) and V3 has two (sites 1 and 2).
I used the following command:

rat.fit1 <-coxph(formula = Surv(time, censura, type ="right")~V1*V5+frailty

messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Marc Feldesman and support from Insightful for their answers.

I had warning message with discrim() when doing a linear discriminant
analysis with 3 groups of 10 observations on 12 variables.

In short, the answer is that warning messages are generated by 
discrim() [S+2000] even when the total number of observation is
sufficient to compute the pooled estimate of the covariance
matrix.

Insightful explaind that:

>For discrim() we still compute the QR/SVD/Choleski decomposition on the 
>individual covariances in order to get the log determinant for each
covariance 
>and the group's scaling matrix. This is where the rank difficiency message
is 
>printed.
>
>Note he did not hit the pooled rank deficieny warning
>        if(r < p)
>                warning("Rank deficiency in pooled covariance")"
>

Gabriel Baud-Bovy

messages.subject_clean: class flattening on calling super class methods
messages.body_plain:
I am using S-Plus 6.0 and I want to use object oreintation.

I have the following problem for which, at least I believe, should be a 
simple solution
   ( everyone interested is invited to try it out ) :

#
# beginning of commented example
#

# Say there are classes with names
# PART1, PART2 and GEN, such that 
#
# PART1 extends GEN by direct inclusion and ...
# PART2 extends GEN by direct inclusion
#
# e.g.

setClass( "GEN", representation( x = "integer" ) )

setClass( "PART1", representation( "GEN",  y="character" ) )

setClass( "PART2", representation( "GEN",  z="list" ) )

# Further a method FUN is defined for class GEN that
# does nothing but return a list that
# contains the argument x-times:

setGeneric("FUN", function(obj) standardGeneric("FUN"))

setMethod( "FUN", "GEN", function(obj)
        { 
                r <- list()
                for (i in 1:obj@x)
                {
                        r[[i]] <- obj
                }
                r
        }
)

# Now I create a test object of class PART1 ...

to <- new("PART1", x=5, y="hello")

# ... and call FUN

FUN(to)

#
# end of commented example
#

A list of GEN objects will be returned.
My problem is that upon calling the method for class GEN
the information of the object that is of a particular subclass is lost.

One solution is of course to explicitly define method FUN twice,
for class PART1 and for class PART2.
Alternatively one could define FUN as a global function rather than as 
a method.

In particular applications these solutions might not be wanted. 
Therefore I believe that there is a possibility to tell the method that it 
should not coerce the argument to the general class. 
How can this be done ?

Best

Daniel.

messages.subject: implementation of S4 language features in S-plus 6.0
messages.subject_clean: implementation of S4 language features in S-plus 6.0
messages.body_plain:
I'm a little disappointed with the way the S4 language features are 
implemented in S-plus 6.0 and integrated with the S3 language features.

With S-plus 6.0 it seems we new have the situation where the basic S3 
language constructs that are so useful in programming no longer work as 
expected with at least some S4-style classes.  For example, c() and 
unlist() silently give nonsense results with timeDate objects, and concat() 
(the replacement for c()) works only with a limited number of "..." 
arguments (because of the recursive implementation of concat.two()). This 
means that now to effectively program in S-plus 6.0, we need to know two 
languages (with two class systems and two sets of data-structure 
manipulation primitives), and we need to know a cross-product matrix of 
which language constructs work with which object types.

I have two questions for the list:

(1) are these just teething problems that will be worked out soon, or are 
the languages in S-plus 6.0 and above doomed to be dirty, with more ugly 
quirks than even earlier versions had?

(2) does R do any better in its integration of S4 language features? (These 
are part of the base R in version 1.5, if I understand correctly.)

The remainder of this message just goes into a couple of examples of these 
types of things.

unlist(x, rec=F) does not work on lists of timeDate objects (I'm not sure 
if it works for lists of S4-style objects in general).

> x <- lapply(1:3, function(x) timeDate("2001/01/01")+x)
> x
[[1]]:
[1] 2001/01/02

[[2]]:
[1] 2001/01/03

[[3]]:
[1] 2001/01/04

> unlist(x, rec=F)
 [[1]]:
[[1]][[1]]:
[1] 14977

[[1]][[2]]:
[1] 0

[[2]]:
[1] "julian.day"   "milliseconds"
... <more junk>

# The recommended alternative (from S-plus support) is:
> do.call("concat", x)
[1] 2001/01/02 2001/01/03 2001/01/04

The S-plus support people told me that it was impossible to get unlist() to 
work here (because unlist() already does too much) and suggested that I 
instead use do.call("concat", x).  Although somewhat uglier, this does 
indeed work, at least for lists that are shorter than about 50 elements -- 
with longer lists the recursive implementation of concat exhausts the stack 
frame limit (options("expressions")).  In response to the problem of concat 
with long lists, the S-plus support people suggested I write a special 
function that converts the elements of my list to strings and then use 
unlist() on that, and then convert back to my original objects.  I guess 
with S-plus V8.0 we'll be writing in assembly language :-(

Also, c() on timeDate objects does not work (concat() does):
> concat(x[[1]], x[[3]])
[1] 2001/01/02 2001/01/04
> c(x[[1]], x[[3]])
[[1]]:
[[1]][[1]]:
[1] 14977

[[1]][[2]]:
[1] 0

[[2]]:
[1] "julian.day"   "milliseconds"

... <more junk>

At least unique() still works on timeDate objects!

Another example of an ugly quirk is that it is impossible to write an 
as.character() method for a new style class where that class is defined 
just with a prototype (at least S-plus support didn't know how).

Here's an example of this particular problem:

> setClass("junkClass2", prototype=integer(0))

> setAs("junkClass2", "character", function(object) paste("#", 
as.integer(object)))

> z2<-new("junkClass2", 1:3)

> z2

# An object of class "junkClass2"

[1] 1 2 3
> as(z2, "character")
[1] "# 1" "# 2" "# 3"
> as.character(z2)
[1] "1" "2" "3"
>

Hidden special cases like this of general constructs not working make 
programming painful and error-prone.

(I don't even know whether it is considered valid to define an S4 class 
with just a prototype -- the documentation on S4 classes supplied with 
S-plus 6.0 is so sparse that it's impossible to tell.)

This message is not meant at all to be a complaint about the abilities or 
attitudes of the S-plus support people -- they've been very prompt, polite 
and helpful whenever I've asked questions.  Rather the problems seem to be 
with the design and implementation decisions that were made in integrating 
S4 language constructs and features into S-plus 5 and 6.

-- Tony Plate

messages.body_plain:
S is an evolving language.  It was conceived and designed as an
environment for interacting with data.  Just as the needs and practices
of the statistical community have changed over the years, so has the
language changed to adapt.

S has no defined standard at the moment (like, say, C or Java). S-PLUS's
implementation of S is driven by primarily by the original S
implementation from Bell Labs, plus comments from users and influences
from other languages and statistical packages (including R).  Some
things work well in practice, some things not so well, and the way we
learn which is which is by observation.

Sv4 is a good example of this.  It has some great benefits (notably,
memory management) in addition to providing a new framework for defining
classes and methods.  The designers tried to make the new system as
backwards-compatible as possible, but there are a number of places where
the two class systems clash. In retrospect, perhaps a clean break might
have been easier, but hindsight is 20/20 vision, as they say.

We're working with the user community and experts in the domain to
continue to evolve the S language, to resolve these teething problems,
to improve the utility and elegance of S, and to move towards
convergence in its various implementations.  These things take time:
we've been concentrating recently in implementation bugs in Sv4 in
S-PLUS, and as we move on we'll be able to consider and address design
issues.  The R folks are also working in this direction, and the sum of
our joint experiences will lead to a better language in the future.

As I say, the way we know what works well and what does not is by
observation.  So if you do encounter such problems (such as the failure
of concat for large numbers of arguments, which is a bug), please do let
us know (the easiest way is to email bugs at insightful.com).  The support
team is also there to help you work through any such problems.  We rely
on your input to be able to continue to improve S and S-PLUS.

Thanks,
# David Smith

P.S.  A while back, I wrote an article about the history and usage of
Sv4 in S-PLUS.  It's a little out-of-date now, but it may still be of
interest.  See:
http://www.insightful.com/DocumentsLive/22/26/splus6.pdf

--

> arguments (because of the recursive implementation of 
> concat.two()). This 
> means that now to effectively program in S-plus 6.0, we need 
> to know two 
> languages (with two class systems and two sets of data-structure 
> manipulation primitives), and we need to know a cross-product 
> matrix of 
> which language constructs work with which object types.
> 
> I have two questions for the list:
> 
> (1) are these just teething problems that will be worked out 
> soon, or are 
> the languages in S-plus 6.0 and above doomed to be dirty, 
> with more ugly 
> quirks than even earlier versions had?
> 
> (2) does R do any better in its integration of S4 language 
> features? (These 
> are part of the base R in version 1.5, if I understand correctly.)
> 
> The remainder of this message just goes into a couple of 
> examples of these 
> types of things.
> 
> unlist(x, rec=F) does not work on lists of timeDate objects 
> (I'm not sure 
> if it works for lists of S4-style objects in general).
> 
>  > x <- lapply(1:3, function(x) timeDate("2001/01/01")+x)
>  > x
> [[1]]:
> [1] 2001/01/02
> 
> [[2]]:
> [1] 2001/01/03
> 
> [[3]]:
> [1] 2001/01/04
> 
>  > unlist(x, rec=F)
>   [[1]]:
> [[1]][[1]]:
> [1] 14977
> 
> [[1]][[2]]:
> [1] 0
> 
> 
> [[2]]:
> [1] "julian.day"   "milliseconds"
> ... <more junk>
> 
> # The recommended alternative (from S-plus support) is:
>  > do.call("concat", x)
> [1] 2001/01/02 2001/01/03 2001/01/04
> 
> The S-plus support people told me that it was impossible to 
> get unlist() to 
> work here (because unlist() already does too much) and 
> suggested that I 
> instead use do.call("concat", x).  Although somewhat uglier, 
> this does 
> indeed work, at least for lists that are shorter than about 
> 50 elements -- 
> with longer lists the recursive implementation of concat 
> exhausts the stack 
> frame limit (options("expressions")).  In response to the 
> problem of concat 
> with long lists, the S-plus support people suggested I write 
> a special 
> function that converts the elements of my list to strings and 
> then use 
> unlist() on that, and then convert back to my original 
> objects.  I guess 
> with S-plus V8.0 we'll be writing in assembly language :-(
> 
> Also, c() on timeDate objects does not work (concat() does):
>  > concat(x[[1]], x[[3]])
> [1] 2001/01/02 2001/01/04
>  > c(x[[1]], x[[3]])
> [[1]]:
> [[1]][[1]]:
> [1] 14977
> 
> [[1]][[2]]:
> [1] 0
> 
> 
> [[2]]:
> [1] "julian.day"   "milliseconds"
> 
> ... <more junk>
> 
> At least unique() still works on timeDate objects!
> 
> Another example of an ugly quirk is that it is impossible to write an 
> as.character() method for a new style class where that class 
> is defined 
> just with a prototype (at least S-plus support didn't know how).
> 
> Here's an example of this particular problem:
> 
>  > setClass("junkClass2", prototype=integer(0))
>  > setAs("junkClass2", "character", function(object) paste("#", 
> as.integer(object)))
>  > z2<-new("junkClass2", 1:3)
>  > z2
> # An object of class "junkClass2"
> 
> [1] 1 2 3
>  > as(z2, "character")
> [1] "# 1" "# 2" "# 3"
>  > as.character(z2)
> [1] "1" "2" "3"
>  >
> 
> Hidden special cases like this of general constructs not working make 
> programming painful and error-prone.
> 
> (I don't even know whether it is considered valid to define 
> an S4 class 
> with just a prototype -- the documentation on S4 classes 
> supplied with 
> S-plus 6.0 is so sparse that it's impossible to tell.)
> 
> This message is not meant at all to be a complaint about the 
> abilities or 
> attitudes of the S-plus support people -- they've been very 
> prompt, polite 
> and helpful whenever I've asked questions.  Rather the 
> problems seem to be 
> with the design and implementation decisions that were made 
> in integrating 
> S4 language constructs and features into S-plus 5 and 6.
> 
> -- Tony Plate
>

> unsubscribe send e-mail to s-news-request at lists.biostat.wustl.edu with
> the BODY of the message:  unsubscribe s-news

messages.subject: Re: class flattening on calling super class methods
messages.subject_clean: class flattening on calling super class methods
messages.body_plain:
This is a good point to raise.

The "flattening" of objects; i.e., actually coercing them to the class
for which the method is defined, is sometimes needed because there may
be an explicit coerce method defined, and the object won't then work as
a GEN object wihout coercing.

But in simple cases, it would be more like other languages and just
generally better to NOT coerce.  I hope that future versions of S-Plus
will work that way  (it's not a big change).

Meanwhile, I think you can get the behavior you want if the GEN class
(in your example) is a VIRTUAL class:  that tells the evaluator it
should not coerce objects to that class.  Changing the first class
definition in your example to

setClass( "GEN", representation("VIRTUAL",  x = "integer" ) )

causes FUN(to) to produce a list of PART1 objects.

Using virtual classes can be slightly inconvenient in that it may
require a few extra classes to be defined, so the modified behavior
would be a nice change.  But you should still be able to get what you
want from the current definition.

messages.subject: Crossvalidation with quadratic discriminant analysis
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-Plus users,

I have encountered a problem with some datasets when
using the crossvalidation option in quadratic discriminant
analysis. This error arises with crossvalidate.discrim() and
qda(, CV=T) and, for some datasets, seems to be platform
dependent (e.g. error on S+2K Pro rel. 3, Win2k but not 
on S+2K Pro rel. 2, Win 98).  This error also arises when
group spherical covariance matrices are specified in discrim().

Looking at the code of crossvalidate.discrim(), the error
seems also to be related to very small negative values in the computation
of the determinant of the covariance matrix that yield NA when
the log is taken.

These error seems to be a numerical problem (which may also
explain why it is platform dependent).

How can I address this problem (I have hundreds of data sets
to classify)? For example, I thought of using zapsmall:

ldet[ind]<-log( zapsmall(1-nc/(nc-1)/(nc-1)*dist[ind])) +
p*log((nc-1)/(nc-2)) + ldet[ind]

Thank you for any suggestion.

Gabriel Baud-Bovy

PS: To illustrate the problem, I attached one of the
problematic datasets (4 variables, 3 groups of 10 observations) 
to this post.

data.restore("dumpdata")

fit<-discrim(ep~.,data=data0,family=Classical("hetero"))
crossvalidate(fit)
Error in FUN: Missing value where logical needed: if(m < doubt) return(k + 1)

qda(ep~.,data0,CV=T)

messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I'm trying to run simulations where I simulate some data from an Emax model,
add residual variability and then fit an nls function to it.  I know in some
cases my choice of sample size will result in nls not being able to fit the
data successfully for the given parameters.  Is there a way that I can avoid
the loop bombing out when nls fails, but rather store a flag?  The question
I'm trying to answer is how many "trials" I simulate can estimate the Emax
parameters I put in in the first place for a given sample size?

I'd really appreciate some help.

Cheers,
Mike

############################################################################
##########

 Inhib.fn<-function(Emax, E0, ED50, Dose,gamma=1)
{
        y <- E0 - (E0-Emax) * (Dose^gamma/(Dose^gamma + ED50^gamma))
        y
}

sim<-function(ns,ED50.mean,gamma){

dose.lev<-c(0,20,40,80)
dose<-sample(dose.lev,ns,replace=T)
E0.mean<-40
Emax.mean<-30

gamma<-rep(gamma,ns)
ED50<-rep(ED50.mean,ns)
E0<-rnorm(ns,E0.mean,11.28)
E0<-ifelse(E0<0,0,E0)
Emax<-rnorm(ns,Emax.mean,13.62)
error<-rnorm(ns,0,1.60)

gen<-Inhib.fn(Emax,E0,ED50,dose,gamma)

obs<-gen+error
FOO<-data.frame(cbind(obs,Emax,E0,ED50,gamma,dose))
FOO$subjid<-c(1:ns)

## This will help illustrate what I mean but isn't required for the
simulation!
#mean.obs<-tapply(obs,dose,mean)
#plot(FOO$dose,FOO$obs)
#lines(dose.lev,mean.obs,col=6)
#lines(c(1:50),Inhib.fn(Emax.mean,E0.mean,ED50.mean,c(1:50)),col=8)

model.nls<-nls(obs~Inhib.fn(Emax,E0,ED50,dose),data=FOO,start=list(Emax=30,E
0=40,ED50=ED50.mean))
model.nls.sum<-summary(model.nls)
signif<-sum(model.nls.sum$parameters[,3]>pt(0.975,1))
success<-signif>1
}

nls.control(maxiter=100,tolerance=0.00001)
# ns = number of subjects
# question is how many "trials" can estimate the relevant parameters of the
Emax for a given 
# sample size
for (i in 1:100){
        res[i]<-sim(1000,20,1)
}
sum(res)

messages.subject: xyplot?
messages.body_plain:
All,

I recently asked how to add an "extra" line to the second panel
plot in the following code:

> xyplot(c14~I(palk-2320)|ocean,data=palkdf,
>   panel=function(x,y){
>       panel.xyplot(x,y,pch=8)
>       abline(-59,-.962,lwd=2,lty=1)
>       fit_lm(y~x)
>       abline(fit$coef,lty=3)
>       })

Several people suggested solutions using groups and subscripts, however
the most elegant fix was supplied by Jim Pratt who offered the following:
---------------------------
You can get the panel number currently being plotted via

pnl<-get('n',frame=sys.parent())

Then use logical to have it add additional abline for desired panel (by
number)

if (pnl==2) abline(-55,-1.01,col=2)

This would of course all take place within you panel=function set of
statements.

This assumes you know the panel number of interest.
----------------------------
This gives:

 xyplot(c14~I(palk-2320)|ocean,data=palkdf,
   panel=function(x,y){
       panel.xyplot(x,y,pch=8)
       abline(-59,-.962,lwd=2,lty=1)
       fit_lm(y~x)
       abline(fit$coef,lty=3)
       pnl<-get('n',frame=sys.parent())
       if (pnl==2) abline(-55,-1.01,col=2)
       })

messages.body_plain:
S-PLUS6 R2, Windows 2000

This is more of a statistics question, but I need to know what S-PLUS commands 
to use also.  I have a bunch of wind speed data, namely the 5-minute average 
speed and the peak gust speed within the 5-minute period.  I need to determine 
the probability of reaching certain gust speed given a certain average speed.  
I've been using the Robust library functions and finding that the Gamma and 
Weibull MLE distributions fit the gust speed pdf's rather well.  As all good 
Gamma and Weibull distributions should, the left tail of the pdf goes to 0.  
The problem is that when the average speed is, say, 20 knots, the probability 
of the gust being less than 20 should be 0.  In other words, the tail should go 
to 0, or very close to it, at 20 knots.  As a first guess, I took all of the 
gust speeds observed when the average speed was 20 (345 observations) and fit 
the MLE and Robust models to the data using:

> spd20.fit <- fit.models(list(mle="gammaMLE", robust="gammaRob"), data=spd20)
> summary(spd20.fit)
Calls: 
   mle : gammaMLE(data = pspd)
robust : gammaRob(data = pspd)

Coefficients:
               Estimates       SE 
   mle : Alpha 139.9504    0.0153
robust : Alpha  89.7958    0.0294
   mle : Sigma   0.2005   10.6430
robust : Sigma   0.3123    8.4188
   mle :    Mu  28.0638    0.1277
robust :    Mu  28.0406    0.1652

I then subtracted 20 from each of the gust values in spd20 to 'adjust' the data 
to 0, since the minimum gust must be 20:
> spdDiff <- spd20-20
> spdDiff.fit <- fit.models(list(mle="gammaMLE", robust="gammRob"), 
> data=spdDiff)
> summary(spdDiff.fit)

messages.subject: Multiplication
messages.body_plain:
Dear s-users,

I was wondering if anyone have accounted the same oddity with v6.0 as I. 
When I multiply two numbers (stored as integers) and the answer is above 
1e+10 (stored as numeric) the output is "NA". This occurs both when I use 
multiplication "*" and addition "+" of two integers with answer greater 
than 1e+10. However, if on of the numbers are stored as a numeric value the 
multiplication works. Thus, can anyone please tell me why ordinary 
multiplication does not work in the case of 100000000*100, whereas 
10000000000*10 do work.

Below I have given some examples of when I find the multiplication to work 
and when it did not work.

 x<-100000000

> x*10

[1] 1000000000

> x*100

[1] NA

> x*1e+2

[1] 1e+010

> x^2

[1] 1e+016

> x<-10000000000
> x*100
[1] 1e+012

 > x
[1] 1000000000
> x*3
[1] NA
> as.numeric(x)*3
[1] 3e+009

> x+x+x
[1] NA
> as.numeric(x)+x+x
[1] 3e+009

It seems to me that there is a problem in the transition between an 
"integer" and a "numeric" value,i.e. for multiplication of two integers (x 
& x1) where the answer would be stored as a numeric value (x*x1>=1e+10) the 
program gives NA as an output.

I accoutered the problem when I was viewing a kendall rank correlation 
(cor.test(x,y,method="k")), and I had numerous ties in both vectors (x & 
y), in the test I found that the normal-z = NA, this was backtracked to the 
multiplication of t1 and t2 in the vark function (within cor.test):

                t1 <- sum(ties.x * (ties.x - 1) * (ties.x - 2))
                t2 <- sum(ties.y * (ties.y - 1) * (ties.y - 2))
                v2 <- (t1 * t2)/(9 * n * (n - 1) * (n - 2))

In this case t1 and t2 is stored as integers, and the multiplication did 
not work as the answer was above 1+e10, and both t1 and t2 was below 1e+10, 
v2 was then NA. However, in this case we can  adjust by storing either t1 
or t2 as.numeric.

                t1 <- as.numeric(sum(ties.x * (ties.x - 1) * (ties.x - 2)))
                t2 <- sum(ties.y * (ties.y - 1) * (ties.y - 2))
                v2 <- (t1 * t2)/(9 * n * (n - 1) * (n - 2))

With this adjustment it works, and a normal-z is obtained.

Can anyone please explain to me what is happening, and is this a general 
problem for v6.0?

Is there a simple way for me to avoid this complication?

Best wishes,
Your sincerely

Einar Heegaard

messages.subject: Re: Multiplication
messages.body_plain:
If you want real numbers, use 1000000000. etc, just as you would in C or
most other languages.  1e+9 would be easier for everyone, and also works.
You need to tell S-PLUS >= 5 that when you write an integer, you meant a
real.

100000000*100 is an integer larger than the largest repesentable integer
*on your system* (which is 32-bit Windows, as only that uses two
unnecessary zeroes in 3e+009, and hence the largest representable is 2^31 -
1, about 2.1e9).

10000000000 is (again, on your system) converted to a double:
> class(1000000000)
[1] "integer"
> class(10000000000)
[1] "numeric"
tells you what is going on.

 If you wish that parameter a in

messages.subject: Nesting data appropriately in GLM's and appropriate degrees of freedom
messages.subject_clean: Nesting data appropriately in GLM's and appropriate degrees of freedom
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
    I'm trying to model count data that is hierarchical with GLM's using 
quasi-likelihood estimation.  I'm trying to predict tree regeneration as a 
function of two fire treatments, distance from seed source, other tree species 
effects, and number of seed trees in each seed source.  My data are from 6 
plots located within each stand (stand is my replicate) for each treatment.  
The model I've used to reflect the nesting structure is:

Nested <-glm (Density ~ Treatment/Stand + poly(seedtree, 3) + direction
              + Distance + spruce + aspen, family = quasi(link = "log", var =
              "mu"), na.action = na.omit, data=mast, maxit = 20)

Questions:  
1) The predictor variables "seed tree", "direction", "spruce", and "aspen" 
describe the "Stand" replicate (i.e. one value associated with each stand) - 
would the Nesting structure as specified recognize this appropriately when 
looking at the effects of these variables on "density"?

2) I would like to further nest the model by site : i.e. Treatment/Stand/Site, 
since 3 plots are located in each of 2 sites, in each stand.  Running the 
model with this added level of nesting gave this error message:
Error in model.matrix.default(Terms, m..: Trying to allocate a vector with too 
many elements (22980124)

Does this mean I ran out of degrees of freedom?  Is there another way to 
account for the site effect?

2) My degrees of freedom is based on all my plots in the model so it appears 
that I am pseudo replicating (since stand is the replicate).  However, in 
order to account for the levels of nesting, I needed to include them to ensure 
I still had some degrees of freedom.  The plot data also add an important 
level of varience - Is there a way to account for this varience while still 
being able to nest, and not pseudoreplicate?

My output is:
Quasi-likelihood model

Response: Dens2m

Terms added sequentially (first to last)
                   Df Deviance Resid. Df Resid. Dev
              NULL                   577   1448.678
           Treatmt  1 102.3003       576   1346.378
   poly(seedtr, 3)  3  72.0514       573   1274.326
          Directio  6  88.7348       567   1185.591
          Distance  1  29.4650       566   1156.126
           spruce   1  41.6466       565   1114.480
           aspen    1  13.9473       564   1100.532
Stand %in% Treatmt 95 365.6073       469    734.925

Any feedback is appreciated.

Vern Peters

messages.subject: sequential t-test - replies
messages.body_plain:
[my original message to s-news & r-help is attached ]

No one possessed or knew of any S/R code for the sequential t-test.  Also it doesn't appear in the SAS index.

One or two suggested obtaining the S+ seqtrial software which may (or may not) cover this, but this seemed to be a bit of a "hammer to crack a nut".  

I have written a function based on the treatment in Wetheril and Glazebrook 'Sequential Methods in Statistics', which seems to reproduce the published tables OK (eg, table L in O.L.Davies Design and Analysis of Industrial Experiments).

The function is neither elegant nor fast, but anyone is free to make use of it ... there being no guarantees or support with it, of course.

                cheers                Bob

Code follows  ...

function(delta = 1, alpha = 0.05, beta = 0.05, minn = 1, maxn = 20, bot = -10, top = 10)

{

        # Create tables and graphs for Barnard's SPRT ("sequential t-test") 

        # (a) uses expressions given in Wetherill & Glazebrook 'Sequential Methods in Statistics', p 60

        # (b) succesfully reproduces table L in OL Davies Design & Analysis of Industrial Experiments'

        #

        # notation is a mixture of a and b.

        #

        # delta is the difference-to-detect ( in std devs )

        # alpha, beta are the reqd type1 & 2 errors

        # minn:maxn is the range of sample-numbers

        # bot:top is the range used in solving for critical values

        #

        #

        Hh <- function(N = 5, X = 0, lolim = 0, hilim = Inf)

        {

                # an integral required in the likelehood ratio

                #

                integrand <- function(y, n, x)

                {

                        ans <- ((y^n) * exp(-0.5 * (x + y)^2))/gamma(n + 1)

                        ans

                }

                a <- integrate(f = integrand, lower = lolim, upper = hilim, subdivisions = 500, n = N, x = X)

                a$integral

        }

        #

        #

        Lik <- function(U, N, DELTA, lhs)

        {

                # roots of this function are the critical values ( 'U0' and 'U1' in Davies )

                #

                lik <- lhs - (exp(-0.5 * (DELTA^2) * (N - U^2)) * Hh(N - 1,  - DELTA * U))/Hh(N - 1)

                lik

        }

        #

        #

        # 

        U0 <- U1 <- rep(NA, maxn)

        #

        SampNo <- 1:maxn

        #

        # for each n in the required sequence, get the critical values U0 and U1

        #

        for(n in minn:maxn) {

                U1[n] <- uniroot(Lik, lower = bot, upper = top, N = n, DELTA = delta, lhs = (1 - beta)/alpha)$root

                U0[n] <- uniroot(Lik, lower = bot, upper = top, N = n, DELTA = delta, lhs = beta/(1 - alpha))$root

                cat("\n", n, "\t", U0[n], "\t", U1[n])

        }

        #

        # make a plot to provide hard-copy for users

        #

        ttl <- paste("delta=", delta, "alpha=", alpha, "beta=", beta)

        yr <- range(na.omit(c(U0, U1)))

        #        dyr <- max(yr) - min(yr)

        #        yr <- c(yr[1] - 0.2 * dyr, yr[2] + 0.2 * dyr)

        pyr <- pretty(yr)

        plot(c(1, maxn), yr, type = "n", xlab = "Sample no.", ylab = "", main = ttl)

        lines(1:maxn, U0, lwd = 5, col = 13)

        lines(1:maxn, U1, lwd = 5, col = 13)

        text(1, U1[1], "Difference detected")

        text(1, U0[1], "Difference not detected")

        abline(v = seq(1:maxn), h = pyr)

        #

        # table as in Davies

        #

        ans <- data.frame(cbind(SampNo, U0, U1))

        ans

}

           

................................

Does anyone have, or know of, some S or R code to implement

The test is outlined in Kendall & Stuart vol 2A, ch 24, and a 'how

messages.subject: Summary: New graphsheet with plot()
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Leonid Gibiansky, Bert Gunter, Chuck Taylor, and Karl Nissen.

Based on all the advice, the best solution for me is to issue the graphsheet() 
function command with no arguments to open a new graphics window for the next 
plot() command.  To quote Bert, "That's just the way S works."  The 'every 
page' option is not what I wanted, but it is nice to do if you want to have 
tabbed graphics in the same graphsheet.  Here is some of the advice concerning 
that:

B. Gunter: "You can set the "every graph" option from somewhere in the 
"options" menus (I forget where exactly -- you'll find it)."

C. Taylor: "Under the Options menu select "Graph Options".  Then change the 
"Auto Pages" field to "Every Graph"."

K. Nissen: "Be aware that the GUI created graphsheet (guiCreate()) does not 
produce the same object as the graphsheet() call. The graphs produced have 
different characteristics, and the management tools (eg gr.next) only work on 
graphs produced by the individual graphsheet functions. This is a bit hazy as I 
don't have the code (or S-plus) on my computer at the moment.  eg gr.next will 
only work with graphsheet() created graphs."

Again, thanks to everyone.

W

messages.subject: Summary: Weibull and other distributions
messages.body_plain:
I got some quick and helpful answers to my distribution question.  Thanks to 
Charles Annis, Kim Elmore, and P.J. Wells for their help.  The original email 
was rather long, so rather than clutter this email with all that text I suggest 
going back and reading it (Subject: Weibull and other distributions).

Here is a quick summary.  I have 7 years of wind speed and gust data sampled 
every 5 minutes.  I am trying to determine the distribution of gusts associated 
with certain average speeds.  For example, for all average 5-minute speeds of 
20 knots, a range of gusts from 24-36 knots have been recorded.  The empirical 
probability distribution looks very much like a gamma or Weibull distribution 
with a short tail on the left (lower values) and a long tail out to the right 
(higher values).  When fitting a theoretical distribution to these data, 
however, the left tail goes all the way to 0, resulting in probability of 
occurrence of gusts less than 20 knots occurring when the average speed is 20 
knots.  As any good meteorologist knows, the very definition of a gust 
*requires* that it be higher than the average speed.  My solution was to 
subtract the average speed of 20 knots from every gust observation, resulting 
in a gust range of 4-16 knots.  Fitting a theoretical distribution to this data 
caused the probabilities to go to 0 at 0, resulting in a better fit compared to 
the empirical pdf.  I could then just at 20 to the values on the x-axis of the 
pdf to get the probability of occurrence for each of the original gust values.

I did not know, however, if this was 'legal' to do statistically, and asked 
about a 3-parameter Weibull distribution procedure in S-PLUS.  The gist of the 
responses is that what I did could be considered a 3-parameter distribution, 
since the third parameter is an offset.

Chuck Annis adds other information that did not pertain to my problem, but it 
may to others so I will include it here:

>>What you have described is indeed the 3-parameter Weibull, and it appears 
>>that using it as you report is OK because you aren't interested in the left 
>>hand part of the density.  The Big problem with the third parameter is that 
>>you have *defined* the probability of being less than x-zero (the third 
>>parameter) to be zero.  In your case with wind speeds it may be acceptable 
>>that there is some finite probability of a wind speed of, say 19 mph, even 
>>though you have defined it to be zero, not merely small.  If, however, you 
>>are concerned with windspeeds in that region, then defining your problem away 
>>with a third parameter would be dangerous.  Another item comes to mind:  You 
>>have assumed that x-zero is a single-valued, fixed constant.  What if it is 
>>not a constant=20 mph, but rather has some probability density centered at 
>>20?  (One trouble with the constant is that all future readings must be 
>>greater than 20 since subtracting 20 from a future reading of say, 19, would 
>>violate the requirement that Weibull be defined such that x>0.)  Pascual and 
>>Meeker looked at a similar situation with fatigue runout, which for years had 
>>been treated as an asymptotic constant, not unlike what you are doing with 
>>your min windspeed.  They treated the runout, not as a constant, but as a 
>>density, and were able to model fatigue data much more effectively that had 
>>been before.  You may wish to read their paper: (Pascual and Meeker, 
>>"Estimating Fatigue Curves with the Random Fatigue-Limit Model," 
>>TECHNOMETRICS Vol. 41, No. 4, p.277-302, November 1999).<<

Dr. Kim Elmore, a fellow meteorologist, sent this advice and a wonderful 
tutorial which I have attached to this email:

>>I'd guess that this is OK.  What you've done is generate a distribution that 
>>describes the probability of a gust that is "delta" above the mean, where the 
>>mean (in your example) is 20.  The Weibull distribution *does* have three 
>>parameters, though most of the time, the location parameter is ignored.  All 
>>it does is offset the distribution along the horizontal axis, so that the 
>>distribution has zero density below a certain value.  If this parameter is 
>>implicitly zero (as I believe it is in S-Plus) the you should model the gust 
>>value as a delta above the mean, so gusts to 25 with a mean wind of 20 should 
>>have a gust value of 5.<<
As far as the attachments go, they come from the documentation for a regression 
package for Mac computers called "Regress+" developed by Dr. Michael P. 
McLaughlin.  His work states that it may be freely distributed, but it is 
*copyrighted* and may not be sold in whole or in part.  It also must be 
attributed when used.  The details about the Weibull distribution are in the 
Appendix.  It looks like a fun read.

P.J. Wells sent some advice that I can't use since I don't have Environmental 
Stats, but it may be helpful to someone out there:

>>If you have or can get the EnvironmentalStats for S-Plus module, I strongly 
>>suggest using L-moments (which the module provides methods for) to estimate 
>>location/scale/shape distributional models, using the recipes in "Regional 
>>Frequency Analysis" by Hosking and Wallis (1997).  MLE appears to be useless 
>>as a method for finding thresholds -- it jus homes in on the minimum observed 
>>value.  L-moments don't suffer from the problems which vitiate ordinary 
>>method-of-moments, and the location parameter (and hence threshold or offset 
>>values, where these are not directly the parameters) and the other parameters 
>>are simply estimated by polynomials of the L-moment ratios.  There are 
>>several wind-speed examples in Hosking and Wallis's book.<<

Thanks for all the great information, and I hope this email helps others out 
there.

messages.subject: Re: Troubles with gamma distribution
messages.body_plain:
Paul, Bob, Tim, Charles, et al.

I did not express myself as well as I should have.

First, I am using SPlus 6, rel 2 on Win 98.

Second, The 1/2^n sequence I used is itself irrelevant to the problem.  I could have used any decreasing sequence.  I am not confusing rate and scale.  The 1/2^n was for demonstration only.

Third, if I set the parameters \alpha and \beta equal to each other, then the mean is \alpha/\beta = 1, the variance is \alpha/\beta^2 = 1/beta, the skewness is 2/sqrt(\alpha), and the kurtosis is 6/\alpha.  Thus, under these conditions  and as \alpha and \beta (constrained to be equal) go to 0, the mean of the gamma dist remains fixed at 1 and the variance, skewness, and kurtosis increase without bound.  Because the support is bounded below at zero, this means that the density is being spread out more and more from zero towards infinity. This in turn means that a given quantile, e.g., 95%, should also move toward infinity as \alpha and \beta go to infinity.

Thus the behavior of the qgamma function does not agree with my (admittedly informal) reasoning.  Which is wrong?  Bob's confirmation of SPLUS's behavior with Mathematica's suggests my reasoning is incorrect, but I don't see it.

I appreciate all the comments.

Joe

messages.subject: LME Simulation and Memory
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I'm using lme() in a series of simulations. I'm finding memory usage is
shooting through the roof as the simulation iterates --- despite my best
efforts to implement the advice in "S Programming"(V&R) and the
"Programmer's Guide" to Splus 6.0 Release 1 for Linux. The platform is
Debian (woody) Linux, 2xAthlon 1.4Ghz CPU, 1GB RAM, NLME version 3.3.1.

The code I include below looks like a mess because I've tried to
assign() and get() everything directly from the working database in an
effort to prevent for() from keeping everything in memory. Somehow
this doesn't work -- and just seems to make my code ugly!

----------------------a snippet of the code-------------------
sims<-seq(1,100,1) #Specify 100 simulations

##Make 100 data frames [each one 1800x5], and collect them in a big list
DESdat<-lapply(sims,FUN=function(x) ... make data frame here...)

mycov<-matrix(c(.09,-.01,-.01,.0075),2,2) #Cov Matrix of Random Effects

for(i in sims){
## lme() with pre-specified cov matrix of mycov using the ith
## dataframe in DESdat

  assign("DES.all",lme(Y~X+Z1+Z2+Z1:X+Z2:X,
                        data=get("DESdat",immediate=T,where=1)[[i]],
                        random=list(CD = pdSymm(mycov,form=~X)), 
                        
control=list(msMaxIter=0,niterEM=0)),immediate=T,where=1)

## Since the first run of lme doesn't return the correct cov matrix,
## iterate a few times, updating the cov matrix each time.
  for(j in 1:10){
    assign("DES.all",update(get("DES.all",immediate=T,where=1),
           
random=list(CD=pdSymm(mycov/get("DES.all",immediate=T,where=1)$sigma^2,
                  form=~X))),immediate=T,where=1)
     NULL
                 }

##Collect results from the model into a list
  assign("junkmat",
   list(i,
      bs=summary(get("DES.all",immediate=T,where=1))$tTable[,1],
      ses=summary(get("DES.all",immediate=T,where=1))$tTable[,2],
      stdDev=(get("DES.all",immediate=T,where=1)$sigma*attr(junksum,"stdDev")),
      Sigma=get("DES.all",immediate=T,where=1)$sigma),
      immediate=T,where=1)
  
##Write one line to the results file 
  write.table(matrix(unlist(get("junkmat",immediate=T,where=1)),nrow=1),
    file="sims.csv",append=T,sep=",",dimnames.write=F,quote.strings=F)

  print(simnum) #Print simulation number so I can see what is going on
  
##Try to recapture some memory by removing objects and returning NULL
  remove(c("DES.all","junkmat"),frame=sys.nframe())
  NULL
} 

-----------code snippet ends---------------

Any help would be greatly appreciatd!

Thanks!!

Jake 

-----
Jake Bowers
Dept of Political Science
UC-Berkeley

messages.subject: Troubles with gamma distribution -- final statement
messages.subject_clean: Troubles with gamma distribution -- final statement
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Paul, Tim, Bob, Charles, Don, and Glen:

I have finally convinced myself that my troubles with the gamma distribution were of my own making and not those of SPLUS.  Comparisons between SPLUS and Mathematica, plus some basic hard math, have convinced me that the SPLUS routines are indeed correct. Tim, especially, beat me in the head until I understood better what was happening. In particular, my moment-based arguments presented earlier were fallacious. Thanks, Tim.

As \alpha and \beta converge to zero, the gamma density function also converges to zero everywhere but at zero.  Because the gamma function is continuous, the non-convergence at x=0 entrails non-uniform convergence in intervals near zero.  This non-uniform convergence depends exquisitely on the actual course \alpha and \beta take in their paths to 0.  Not knowing this, and assuming roughly uniform convergence was the source of my mistaken reasoning.

Joe
